Case Study

Wake County SPCA

Redesigning the Adoption Process

Role
UX Researcher & Designer
Type
Personal Project
Timeline
2022, 2023
Tools
Figma · Maze · Miro

Overview

The Challenge

As a self-initiated project, I identified a real usability problem: the Wake County SPCA's existing website made it difficult for prospective adopters to find animals, understand the process, or feel confident taking the next step.

I took it as a design challenge, reimagining the adoption experience from browsing pets to scheduling an appointment, with a focus on clarity, compassion, and accessibility across devices.

Key Goals

01

Reduce friction in finding and filtering adoptable pets by temperament, size, and energy level

02

Make shelter info (hours, location, fees, policies) easy to find and trust

03

Simplify appointment scheduling and clarify pet availability statuses

04

Design a compassionate experience that works seamlessly on mobile and desktop

Constraints

Designing Without a Real Backend

This was a self initiated project with no access to the shelter's real backend, CMS, or stakeholders. Every decision was validated through self run usability testing in Maze rather than live traffic, and the redesign had to stay realistic enough for a volunteer run, low budget operation to actually build.

User Research

User Personas

Through user interviews and surveys, I identified two primary adopter archetypes with distinct needs, mental models, and pain points.

Outcomes

Impact & Key Decisions

4
Clear service pathways, Adopt, Foster, Donate, Volunteer, visible above the fold
2×
Reduction in steps to find and filter an adoptable pet
100%
Mobile-responsive design, optimized for phone-first browsing patterns

Conclusions

Key Findings

01

Emotional resonance drives adoption intent

Users responded most strongly to pet personality tags and expressive photos placed above the fold. Surfacing these details earlier before asking for any commitment significantly increased engagement with pet profiles.

02

Navigation ambiguity caused early drop-off

In the original site, most users missed the "Adopt" entry point entirely and exited before reaching any pet listings. Consolidating the four core services (Adopt, Foster, Donate, Volunteer) into clearly labeled, persistent navigation paths resolved this consistently across usability sessions.

03

Mobile users were underserved by the original design

Browsing patterns skewed heavily toward mobile, yet the original layout required desktop-style horizontal scrolling and small tap targets. Rebuilding with a mobile-first grid and larger interactive zones reduced friction immediately.

04

Form length created perceived barriers

The original 7-page adoption application felt opaque and open-ended. Restructuring it into labeled, numbered steps with visible progress reduced anxiety and made the process feel manageable even before the total length changed.

Trade-offs

Alternatives Considered

01

A matchmaking quiz, or straightforward filters?

We considered a custom matchmaking quiz to recommend pets, but chose straightforward filtering by temperament, size, and energy instead. A quiz would have added more ongoing maintenance than a volunteer run shelter could realistically sustain.

02

Shorten the form, or restructure it?

We considered shortening the seven page adoption application, but chose to restructure it into labeled, progress tracked steps first. Required questions likely couldn't be cut, so this traded fewer questions for less perceived friction.

03

A native app, or a responsive site?

We considered a native mobile app, but chose a responsive, mobile first website instead. That matched how people were already browsing without asking a small nonprofit to build and maintain an app.

Future Iterations

What to Test Next

Filter UX

A/B test filter panel placement top bar vs. collapsible sidebar to measure which layout drives more pet profile views and fewer abandoned searches.

Application Flow

Instrument the multi-step adoption form to track per-step drop-off rates. Use findings to determine whether step count, copy clarity, or required fields are the primary friction points.

Alerts & Retention

Prototype and test a "notify me" opt-in that alerts users when a new pet matching their saved filters becomes available targeting users who browse but don't complete an application.

Foster Pathway

Design and test a dedicated foster-first flow to lower the commitment barrier for users who express interest in adoption but hesitate at permanent placement.

Accessibility

Conduct a full WCAG 2.1 AA audit covering color contrast ratios, keyboard navigation order, and screen reader label accuracy particularly across the filter controls and pet card grid.
